   "mu5": Thinking backwards, are there few ways this business could fail?
   "reinvest": Can it reinvest its profits at high returns for many years?

   "ly3": Is the price/earnings ratio at or below the earnings growth rate?

   "ly7": Are insiders buying and is the company reducing its share count?
   "ly8": Is it overlooked by Wall Street or in a 'boring' niche?

   "fi3": Does its R&D spending produce results?
   "fi4": Is it unusually good at selling?
   "longterm": Does management put long-term value and innovation ahead of short-term profit?
   "gr1": Is it a large, established company?
   "ni10": Has it been profitable in each of the last ten years?
   "gr4": Has it paid a dividend every year for at least 20 years?
   "eps10": Has earnings per share grown by at least one third over ten years?
   "gr6": Is the share price no more than about 15 times average earnings?
   "gr7": Is price/earnings × price/book no more than about 22.5?
   "th1": Does it have proprietary technology about ten times better than the next best?
   "timing": Is the technology and market timing right for this business now?
   "th3": Did it start with a big share of a small market, and can it expand from there?
   "team": Is it led by an exceptional founder or world-class management team?
   "th5": Does it have a way to reach and sell to customers, not just a product?
   "durable": Will its market position still hold in 10 to 20 years, resisting disruption and obsolescence?
   "th7": Has it found a unique opportunity that others don't see?
   "trend": Is it a leading beneficiary of a major platform shift or secular trend (such as AI or cloud computing)?
   "dr1": Are earnings accelerating and analysts' estimates moving up?
   "dr2": Will the business look better in 18–24 months than today, beyond what is already obvious?
   "dr4": Do interest rates, central-bank liquidity and the economy work in its favour?
   "dr6": Are there identifiable events that could drive results higher?
   "dr7": Is conviction high enough that it could be a large, concentrated position?
   "gm": Is the gross margin high, a sign of pricing power?
   "fcfyield": Is the free-cash-flow yield reasonable or attractive for its quality and growth?
   "gb2": Is operating profit high compared with the whole company's value (enterprise value)?
   "pa2": Is the business or industry going through a temporary, fixable setback?
   "pa4": Is the chance of permanent loss small even if the outcome is uncertain?
   "wo1": Is it a leader in AI, robotics, energy storage, blockchain or multiomic sequencing?
   "wo2": Are its product costs falling quickly as volumes grow, opening up big new demand?
   "wo3": Does it combine several innovation platforms?
   "wo4": Could its addressable market be many times larger in five years?
   "ac3": Is it largely insulated from commodity prices, interest rates and similar outside forces?
   "ns1": Does it pass the savings from its growing size back to customers, making it ever harder to compete with?
   "ns4": Is its likely position in 10–20 years clearly stronger than today?
   "va2": Does the product solve a large, painful problem?
   "tn1": Does it sell into a real secular trend (like AI, energy or robotics; ideally the infrastructure layer), as a company built for that trend rather than an old business retrofitting?
   "tn2": Is there a gap between the story the market tells about the company and what it is actually becoming (like Palantir seen as a consultancy, Tesla as a car company)?
   "tn3": Is it outside the zones to avoid: small caps, Chinese companies, commodity producers, airlines, seasonal businesses and startups?
   "tn4": Of these three, does it pass at least two (and have a valid reason for any miss, such as infrastructure needing leverage or a clear path to profit): revenue grown for the past few years, profitable, more cash than debt?
   "tn5": Has free cash flow been positive, and cash exceeded debt, in each of the last 4 to 6 quarters?
   "tn6": Is revenue growing at 10% a year or more?
   "tn7": Is revenue growth % plus free-cash-flow margin % at least 40?
   "tn8": Over the last year, did revenue grow faster than total operating expenses?
   "tn9": Does it avoid every instant kill: market cap under $1B, more debt than cash, short interest above 10%, operating margin below 20%, revenue growth below 10% and falling, two or more earnings misses in the last 4 quarters, or less than 10 years since founding?
   "tn10": Is it free of any major regulatory or legal threat?
   "tn11": Can it be stated plainly as “provides X that helps Y achieve Z, and charges [revenue model]”, with a clear answer to what pain it cures, who is in pain, and why customers choose it over competitors?
   "tn13": Score it on Nash's 13 categories, 0, 5 or 10 each, using the last twelve months: cash vs debt (more debt / more cash / 2x+ cash), revenue growth (<10% / 10-20% / >20%), operating margin (<10% / 10-25% / >25%), short interest (>10% / 5-10% / <5%), institutional ownership (<30% / 30-60% / >60%), revenue growing faster than expenses (no 0 / yes 10), 5-year return vs the S&P 500 (behind / ahead by 10-20% / ahead by 20%+), and, judged harshly, moat, CEO, recession-proof pricing power, secular trend, culture and mission, talent (none / some / strong). Is the total 75 or more? Give the total in the evidence.
   "tn14": Over the last five years, has revenue grown every year, operating margin expanded, free cash flow been positive and rising, and cash exceeded debt every year?
   "tn15": Would a banker lend to it: interest coverage (operating income ÷ interest) of 4x or more, assets (excluding goodwill) at least 2× liabilities, current ratio of 1 or more, and total liabilities under 4× equity?
   "tn18": Does the CEO have a track record of execution (growth, margins, innovation), skin in the game through open-market share purchases, and 10+ years in the role, ideally as founder?
   "tn20": Has it consistently beaten earnings expectations?
   "tn21": Is it free of every red flag: a clown CEO, a co-CEO structure, an acquisition spree, any suspicion of fraud or accounting problems, an auditor change, declining margins, revenue spiking while inventory piles up, or insiders selling hard while the stock runs?
   "tn22": Does it avoid the hype trap of no revenue, weak fundamentals, constant share sales to raise cash and nonstop media hype?
   "tn24": Working back from today's price, is the growth the price implies below what the company is already delivering?
   "tn25": With Nash's DCF (3-year averages of revenue growth and FCF margin, trimmed growth, 5 years of free cash flow, 4% terminal growth, plus cash minus debt), is the value per share above today's price even at a 12% discount rate?
   "tn26": Using the multiple that fits (forward P/E vs peers for mature companies, hardware and banks; Rule of 40 for software; price to sales vs the industry for unprofitable growth), is it attractive, with a PEG (forward P/E ÷ EPS growth) of 1 or less?

summaries.gardner: BMS is a 140-year-old big-pharma company with flat revenue ($48,194M in 2025 vs $46,385M in 2021), not the leader of an emerging industry, so it fits few Rule Breaker traits. Its newer products (Cobenfy, Camzyos, Breyanzi CAR-T, RayzeBio radiopharmaceuticals) show innovation, but the stock trades near 9 times forward earnings rather than looking 'overvalued'.
summaries.buffett: Patented medicines like Eliquis and Opdivo give BMS strong economics today (2025 free cash flow about $12.8B), but the advantage is time-limited, with US exclusivity for both expected to end around 2028. Heavy acquisition-driven debt ($43,120M at June 30, 2026) and a weak record of turning retained capital into growth make it a poor fit for Buffett's durable-moat, low-debt test despite a low price.
summaries.munger: Munger would value the cheap price and high gross margin but invert on the obvious failure modes: patent expiries, US drug-price controls and expensive deals that have not lifted revenue above about $48B. Drug development is hard to predict, so BMS sits closer to his 'too hard' pile than to a simple great business.
summaries.lynch: Lynch would classify BMS as a stalwart facing a patent cliff, with a story that depends on newer drugs (Growth Portfolio $26,409M in 2025, up 17%) outrunning losses from Revlimid, Eliquis and Opdivo. Its forward P/E near 9 and 2026 EPS growth guidance look reasonable, but long-term earnings are expected to fall, so the PEG case is weak beyond 2026.
summaries.fisher: BMS spends heavily on research ($9,951M in 2025) and has produced first-in-class drugs such as Camzyos and Cobenfy, and its sales organisation built Eliquis into a $14,443M product. Fisher would worry that much of its pipeline was bought rather than discovered and that profit margins swing with large acquired-IPRD charges.
summaries.graham: BMS meets Graham's size and long dividend record tests, but fails his earnings stability and price tests: it lost money in 2020 (-$9,015M) and 2024 (-$8,948M), and price/earnings times price/book is about 72. A defensive investor following The Intelligent Investor would not qualify it.
summaries.thiel: BMS is a scaled incumbent rather than a Zero to One monopoly: its products are protected by patents for limited periods and face direct rivals such as Keytruda, Xarelto and generics. It does have distribution and some first-in-class assets, but no proprietary technology that is ten times better across its business.
summaries.gerstner: Gerstner looks for durable compounders with improving fundamentals; BMS shows improving near-term numbers (Q2 2026 non-GAAP EPS up 40%, 2026 guidance raised to $49.0-50.0B revenue) and cost cuts, but faces declining consensus revenue beyond 2028. It is not tied to the AI or platform shifts he favours.
summaries.druckenmiller: Near-term momentum is positive, with Q2 2026 revenue and EPS well above consensus and guidance raised, and the stock rose from about $46 in October 2025 to $59.75. But the 2028 patent cliff and Medicare price negotiation limit the 18-24 month upside case that would justify a concentrated bet.
summaries.smith: BMS has high gross margins (about 71%) and strong free cash flow, but fails Smith's test of a good company on returns without leverage, consistency and growth, because its moat depends on expiring patents and debt-funded acquisitions. It is cheap, but 'buy good companies' is the binding constraint.
summaries.greenblatt: On Magic Formula terms BMS screens reasonably: 2025 operating income of about $10,002M against an enterprise value of about $154B gives an earnings yield near 6.5%, and returns on tangible capital are high because most assets are goodwill and intangibles. The formula would not see the patent-cliff risk to future earnings.
summaries.akre: Akre's three-legged stool asks for an extraordinary business, talented owner-oriented managers and reinvestment at high rates; BMS has profitable products, but its reinvestment record (Celgene, MyoKardia, Mirati, Karuna, RayzeBio) has not grown revenue above about $48B. Its CEO is a hired executive since 2023, so it fits poorly.
summaries.pabrai: Pabrai might see a beaten-down, cash-generative business with a known, temporary-looking problem, trading near 9 times forward earnings with a free-cash-flow yield around 10%. But the patent cliff is a permanent loss of specific revenue streams, so the 'heads I win, tails I don't lose much' test depends on pipeline success.
summaries.wood: BMS is not an ARK-style disruptive innovator: it is not a leader in AI, robotics, energy storage, blockchain or multiomic sequencing. Its cell therapy and radiopharmaceutical work touches ARK's interest in genomic medicine, but these are small parts of a mature drug portfolio.
summaries.ackman: Ackman wants simple, predictable, free-cash-flow-generative businesses with dominant positions and little leverage; BMS is free-cash-flow rich but not predictable given patent expiries and US pricing policy. Its debt load and acquisition history also cut against his criteria, though the low valuation could attract an activist angle.
summaries.sleep: Nick Sleep favoured scale-economics-shared businesses that grow stronger over decades; BMS instead must replace expiring products every decade and does not pass growing scale savings to customers. Its likely position in 10-20 years is uncertain rather than clearly stronger.
summaries.valentine: Valentine looked for huge markets and products that solve painful problems; BMS's medicines do solve serious problems (strokes, cancer, schizophrenia), but it is a mature public company rather than an early-stage venture riding a new market. The fit is only on the 'painful problem' dimension.
summaries.nash: BMS fails many of Nash's screens: debt exceeds cash, revenue grows well under 10% a year, legal and regulatory pressure on drug pricing is high, and the CEO has been in the role only since 2023. It scores about 65 of 130 on his 13-category scorecard, though a simple DCF puts value near today's price.

momentum.evidence: The stock rose from about $46 in October 2025 to $59.75 on October 16, 2026 (about +30%), but it has fallen from about $67 in August 2026 and is flat versus April 2026.

g4.evidence: CEO Christopher Boerner (since November 2023) has delivered raised 2026 guidance, but BMS has no famous anchor investor and its leadership is a typical big-pharma professional team.

g6.evidence: Analysts mostly rate it a Hold with an average target of $65.63 (28 analysts), and at about 9 times forward earnings it is generally seen as cheap rather than overvalued.

simple.evidence: The business (selling patented prescription drugs) is easy to describe, but judging trial outcomes, patent expiries and drug-pricing policy requires specialist knowledge.

b2.evidence: Results swing widely: net losses of $9,015M in 2020 and $8,948M in 2024 from acquired IPRD charges, and revenue fell in 2022, 2023 and 2025.

integrity.evidence: Management pays a steady dividend ($5,045M in 2025) and discloses patent-expiry estimates openly, but large acquisitions such as Celgene and Karuna have been expensive and have not lifted revenue above about $48B.

b6.evidence: BMS has repeatedly bought growth (Celgene 2019, MyoKardia, Mirati, Karuna, RayzeBio), following the same acquisition-heavy path as big-pharma peers.

roic.evidence: 2025 net income of $7,054M is about 13% of equity plus net debt, but this relies on $45,111M of debt at end-2025 and capital is mostly acquired goodwill and intangibles.

fcf.evidence: 2025 operating cash flow of $14,156M less capex of $1,311M gave free cash flow of $12,845M, well above net income of $7,054M.

b10.evidence: Despite heavy reinvestment through acquisitions, revenue has stayed at $45-48B since 2021 and the stock trades at about 9 times forward earnings.

safety.evidence: A simple DCF (1.5% growth, 27.9% FCF margin, 12% discount) gives about $61 per share versus $59.75, so there is little margin of safety once the 2028 patent cliff is considered.

fairprice.evidence: At $59.75 the stock is about 8.7 times the midpoint of 2026 non-GAAP EPS guidance ($6.75-7.00) and has a free-cash-flow yield near 10.5%, reasonable even for a low-growth drugmaker.

mu5.evidence: There are many ways to lose: US exclusivity for Eliquis and Opdivo expected to end around 2028, Medicare price negotiation, trial failures such as milvexian's stopped ACS trial, and $43,120M of debt.

reinvest.evidence: Newer products are growing (Growth Portfolio up 17% to $26,409M in 2025), but reinvestment largely through costly acquisitions has not delivered overall revenue growth.

ly2.evidence: It is a stalwart going through a patent cliff, with a clear story: can the Growth Portfolio replace Eliquis, Opdivo and Revlimid revenue?

ly3.evidence: Forward P/E of about 8.7 is below the roughly 12% EPS growth implied by 2026 guidance versus 2025, but earnings are expected to fall after 2028.

runway.evidence: Consensus long-range estimates (about $36.4B revenue in 2030 via Tickflow) point to revenue declining from $48,194M in 2025.

ly7.evidence: BMS has not repurchased shares since 2023 ($0 in 2024 and 2025) and diluted shares rose from 2,027M in 2024 to 2,048M in Q2 2026; no notable insider buying was found.

ly8.evidence: BMS is widely covered (28 analysts) but out of favour, with a Hold consensus and a low valuation because of the patent cliff.

fi2.evidence: It is preparing successors such as Cobenfy, Camzyos, Breyanzi, iberdomide (accelerated approval August 2026), mezigdomide (PDUFA May 13, 2027) and RYZ101.

fi3.evidence: R&D of $9,951M in 2025 has produced approvals and positive Phase 3 data (iberdomide, mezigdomide, iza-bren), but setbacks such as the stopped milvexian ACS trial show uneven productivity.

fi4.evidence: Its commercial machine built Eliquis to $14,443M in 2025 and lifted Q2 2026 Eliquis sales 22%, and Breyanzi sales rose 82% in 2025.

longterm.evidence: BMS keeps R&D near $10B a year and raised 2026 operating expense guidance to about $16.5B, but it also runs a productivity programme that cut non-GAAP SG&A 11% in 2025.

gr1.evidence: 2025 revenue was $48,194M and its market value is about $122B.

ni10.evidence: It reported net losses attributable to BMS of $9,015M in 2020 and $8,948M in 2024.

gr4.evidence: BMS has paid dividends every year for decades; cash dividends rose from $4,075M in 2020 to $5,045M in 2025.

eps10.evidence: Diluted EPS rose from $0.93 in 2015 to $3.46 in 2025, though 2020 and 2024 were losses.

gr7.evidence: Trailing GAAP P/E is about 13 (EPS about $4.54) and price/book about 5.5 (equity $22,319M), giving a product near 72.

timing.evidence: Timing is good for some franchises (CAR-T, radiopharmaceuticals, new schizophrenia mechanisms), but its two biggest drugs are approaching loss of exclusivity around 2028.

th3.evidence: BMS grew by acquiring established franchises (Celgene in 2019) rather than dominating a small niche first, although Camzyos did start as the first cardiac myosin inhibitor.

team.evidence: CEO Christopher Boerner (PhD, ex-McKinsey and Genentech) has executed well since 2023, but the team is not widely seen as world-class or founder-led.
